cim: Potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence to address disparities in epilepsy

cim_eredeti: Potential and pitfalls of artificial intelligence to address disparities in epilepsy
szoveg_eredeti:
The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address global disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring through AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. However, this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity. In this Review, we examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges.

Most people with epilepsy live in low-income and middle-income countries, where shortages of neurologists, electroencephalography (EEG) and MRI contribute to large diagnostic and treatment gaps.

Low-cost, open-source EEG systems combined with deep learning models that match expert performance in specific EEG tasks could enable minimally trained health workers to screen for epilepsy in resource-limited settings.

Smartphone-based approaches, including video recordings of seizures and passive analysis of touchscreen interaction dynamics, are candidate tools for screening and monitoring but are not yet established diagnostic tests.

Multimodal and reasoning-capable large language models could integrate clinical histories in local languages with EEG data and explain their reasoning, and affordable open-source models can run offline on local devices.

AI models trained in high-income settings often generalize poorly to other populations, so local data collection, external validation and attention to bias, data protection and cultural applicability are essential.

Responsible implementation requires a phased approach — hardware validation, local model adaptation, clinical trials and sustainable scaling — that strengthens clinical expertise and community-based care.
